records.claim: Wen2020 explicitly uses PCFF ('All MD simulations were performed using LAMMPS with the PCFF force field') and directly validates PCFF for Ultem (4,4'-BPADA+MPD), matching PIMN's own ff_note claim almost exactly: MD Tg (rho(T) method) = 525 K vs experimental 490 K. The paper computes Tg by TWO independent methods on the same simulation data -- rho(T) (specific-volume break) and D(T) (a self-diffusion-based method) -- and these disagree with each other: rho(T) gives 525 K (+7.1% vs exp) while D(T) gives 504 K (+2.9% vs exp). The paper's own text states: 'results on Tg from the D(T) data are closer to and only about 10 to 20 K different from the experimental Tg,' i.e. the authors themselves flag the D(T) method as more accurate than the rho(T) method already recorded in PolyJarvis's ff_note.

Other four etherimides (no matched experimental Tg for PPD variant): BPADA+DDS 542/532/537/520 (rho +4.2%, D +2.3%); BPADA+CDA 516/495/551/473 (rho +9.1%, D +4.7%); 3,3'BPADA+MPD 524/500/528/511 (rho +2.5%, D -2.2%). polymer_names: segmented polyurea-polyurethane hybrid elastomers (IPDI + D2000/D230 diamine hard segments + 24 wt% polyol/polycarbonate/polycaprolactone/PTMEG diol soft segments) -- NOT pure polyurea
records.claim: A 2025 MDPI Polymers paper studies dynamic mechanical properties and energy absorption of what it calls 'polyureas' (PURs) via combined experiment and MD simulation, reporting MD density within 2% of experiment for four variants. However, full-text inspection reveals these are segmented POLYUREA-POLYURETHANE HYBRID elastomers -- built from isophorone diisocyanate (IPDI), diamine chain extenders (D2000, D230), AND macrodiol soft segments (polycarbonate, polycaprolactone, polypropylene glycol, or polytetramethylene ether glycol diols, 'remained at 24 wt%') -- not pure polyurea (urea-linkage-only) chemistry. The force field used is COMPASS, not GAFF or GAFF2: 'The COMPASS force field was chosen for the analog modules Forcite and Amorphous Cell.'

records.title: Dynamic Mechanical Properties and Energy Absorption Capabilities of Polyureas Through Experiments and Molecular Dynamic Simulation
records.relevance: FLAGS A DOUBLE SCOPE MISMATCH, not a corroboration: despite being labeled 'polyureas' in the title, this paper is chemically a urea-urethane hybrid segmented elastomer with substantial (24 wt%) diol soft-segment content -- structurally distinct from PURA's pure-urea-linkage chemistry (the class EMC cannot build, routed to RadonPy/GAFF2_mod specifically because of its {na,c_2} amide-N increment gap). It also uses COMPASS, not GAFF2. The strong density accuracy (<2%) reported here therefore cannot be attributed to GAFF2 or to pure polyurea chemistry, and should not be read as evidence for either.

polymer_names: urea (small molecule, NH2-CO-NH2) -- NOT polyurea; the urea linkage is the repeat-unit-defining functional group shared with PURA's polymer chemistry
records.claim: A dedicated small-molecule study of urea itself (the exact chemical linkage at the core of every polyurea repeat unit) assesses 4 GAFF-family and 5 OPLS-family force field variants against experimental urea crystal lattice parameters, crystal density, cohesive energy, and aqueous-solution properties. GAFF2 specifically (PURA's actual routed force field) OVER-predicts urea crystal density: calculated 1.476 g/cm3 vs experimental 1.375 g/cm3 (+7.4%). The paper's own text states: 'All force fields slightly underestimate a and overestimate c, and the density, rho, is overestimated by all of the force fields,' i.e. this is a consistent, systematic direction across every GAFF and OPLS variant tested, not GAFF2-specific noise. This study is a small-molecule urea CRYSTAL study -- it does not simulate polyurea (the polymer) at all, and crystal-density errors do not necessarily transfer to amorphous-melt density errors.

value.reported_errors: Urea crystal density vs experiment (1.375 g/cm3): GAFF1 1.460 (+6.2%), GAFF2 1.476 (+7.4%), GAFF-D1 1.521 (+10.6%), GAFF-D3 1.460 (+6.2%). All force fields tested (GAFF and OPLS families alike) overestimate density; the paper reports 'the experimental form I crystal density [is overestimated] by 7-19%' across the full set.

records.title: Assessment of GAFF and OPLS Force Fields for Urea: Crystal and Aqueous Solution Properties
records.relevance: The single most directly on-topic finding located for PURA: it is GAFF2 (PURA's actual routed force field), on the exact urea functional group that defines polyurea's repeat unit -- a small-molecule analog in the same spirit as section 6's benzene/toluene benchmark for PS. Important caveat, stated explicitly by the task and preserved here: this is a CRYSTAL density comparison for the monomer compound, not an amorphous bulk-polymer-melt comparison for the polymer -- crystal-packing errors and amorphous-melt errors are not the same quantity and need not share sign or magnitude, so this finding should not be read as a direct GAFF2-polyurea bulk-density prediction.

polymer_names: a fast-curing (thermoset) polyurethane resin system tracked across degree-of-cure (DoC) via topological crosslinking MD -- NOT PolyJarvis's linear/aliphatic TPU chemistry
records.claim: PURT's formal ff_justification_doi is confirmed via CrossRef to be a real, correctly-titled 2026 MDPI Polymers paper on fast-curing polyurethane systems. The paper reports NO liquid, amorphous-melt, or bulk-density/Tg validation of any kind -- its entire quantitative validation is: (1) Table 3, ab initio energy-fit residuals for 5 model compounds (carbonic acid, methyl/dimethyl/phenyl/diphenyl carbonate): RMS total-energy deviation 0.32-0.54 kcal/mol; (2) Tables 1-2, crystal lattice-parameter and lattice-energy comparisons for ethylene carbonate and diphenyl carbonate of 2,2-bis(4-hydroxyphenyl)propane (BPA-PC's carbonate-linked model compound) -- unit-cell edges match experiment to 0.03-0.29 A, lattice energies to 1.1-2.3 kcal/mol; (3) Table 5, dimethyl-carbonate vibrational frequencies vs liquid/vapor IR-Raman spectra, max deviation ~60 cm-1 pre-scaling, close post-scaling; (4) Tables 4/6/7, gas-phase conformational energy differences vs HF/6-31G* and MP2 for dimethyl carbonate, diphenyl carbonate, and 2,2-diphenylpropane (largest deviation ~1 kcal/mol); (5) a single crystal-cluster (7-molecule) ring-flip barrier calculation (~20 kcal/mol, explicitly flagged by the authors themselves as an overestimate due to imposed rigidity). No pure-liquid or amorphous-bulk MD/MC simulation of any polycarbonate, and no density or Tg number of any kind, appears anywhere in the paper.

records.relevance: This is the formal ff_justification_doi field for exactly 4 PCFF-default classes: PCBN (polycarbonates), PSTR (polystyrenics), PAMD (polyamides), and PSFO (polysulfones) -- independently re-verified by reading guides/polymer_rules.json directly, not merely by narrative cross-reference. The other 11 PCFF-routed classes (PKTN, PIMD, POXI, PEST, PSUL, PURT, PANH, PPHS, PACR, PIMN, PVNL) each cite their OWN, different, class-specific DOI as ff_justification_doi -- only a few of their ff_note fields separately mention 'Sun1994' as informal PCFF/CFF93-lineage background, which is a materially weaker claim (general methodology provenance, not chemistry-specific validation evidence) and not the same finding as a mis-citation. For PCBN specifically this DOI is a genuinely on-chemistry founding citation FOR THE PARAMETERIZATION METHODOLOGY, but full-text reading (2026-08-24) shows it is NOT bulk-property validation even for PCBN: it validates conformational energetics and crystal-lattice structure on small model compounds and dimers only, never an amorphous polycarbonate melt's density or Tg. So PCBN's own PCFF density/Tg accuracy is, on this founding paper's evidence alone, just as unvalidated at the bulk-property level as PSTR/PAMD/PSFO's -- the difference between PCBN and the other 3 classes is chemistry-match, not validation depth. For PSTR/PAMD/PSFO it is being used as a stand-in for 'the PCFF/Class-II force field's founding validation,' when the paper's own actual scope (by its title and its ab initio+crystal-structure model-compound methodology) is the polycarbonate structural family only -- an even narrower scope than the generic 'small molecules' extrapolation already documented for COMPASS in section 5. This paper does not itself claim to validate PCFF broadly across chemistries; that broader claim is an assumption made by this codebase's citation practice on 3 classes, not a statement in the source.

methodology_criteria.criterion: Prefer a field with a same-polymer or same-family published benchmark reporting signed density/Tg error against experiment, over a field chosen solely on general reputation.
methodology_criteria.how_to_apply: Before adopting a fallback field for a novel/no-experimental-data polymer, search for any same-polymer or same-family multi-FF benchmark (as in the PDMS and PMMA/PIB cases found here); if none exists, treat the fallback choice as unvalidated rather than assuming general-purpose reputation transfers.

methodology_criteria.criterion: Do not assume atom-type/fragment coverage of a novel chemistry by a force field's parameterization set predicts lower simulated-property error; the literature has not established this relationship, and directly measuring it (as we did, -0.26 K, -0.64 density) is more informative than an a-priori coverage argument.
methodology_criteria.how_to_apply: Treat 'this polymer contains atom types outside the field's training set' as a flag for verification-needed, not as a predictor of error direction or magnitude, when deciding whether to trust a force field on a novel polymer.

methodology_criteria.criterion: When no experimental data exists, use CED/solubility-parameter comparison against Hansen/Hildebrand group-contribution tables as an independent (density/Tg-orthogonal) reference-free check, expecting ~1 Hildebrand-unit discriminating accuracy.
methodology_criteria.how_to_apply: Compute CED from the equilibrated MD cell and compare to a group-contribution-estimated solubility parameter for the polymer's chemistry; treat disagreement beyond ~1-2 Hildebrands as a flag against the force field/parameterization, independent of the density/Tg gates already in use.

methodology_criteria.criterion: Group-contribution Tg estimators (van Krevelen/Bicerano-style, or newer hybrid QSPR-GAP) can serve as a reference-free Tg sanity check to roughly 8-10 K or ~5-10% MRE, but only when the polymer's structural fragments are well represented in the estimator's training set; traditional (non-hybrid) group contribution is explicitly reported to degrade on fragments absent from training data.
methodology_criteria.how_to_apply: Use a group-contribution Tg estimate as a secondary sanity bound on simulated Tg for novel polymers, but discount it (do not treat disagreement as force-field evidence) when the polymer's backbone chemistry is not well represented in the estimator's own training set.

methodology_criteria.criterion: A known systematic force-field bias (e.g., a class-wide density deficit) does not by itself justify switching fields; the largest-scale published pipeline (RadonPy) response to an admitted systematic GAFF2 density bias was a statistical/ML post-hoc correction, not a per-chemistry field switch.
methodology_criteria.how_to_apply: If a systematic, well-characterized bias is found (as with our measured -5.9% PCFF density deficit), consider a calibrated post-hoc correction as a literature-precedented alternative to switching to an unvalidated fallback field, especially when the fallback field (e.g. GAFF2 for aromatic backbones) itself lacks chemistry-specific bulk validation.

methodology_criteria.criterion: High-throughput pipelines in the literature fix one force field for an entire cross-chemistry screening campaign rather than performing automated per-polymer force-field selection; there is no published precedent for a per-chemistry FF-selection algorithm to cite or emulate.
methodology_criteria.how_to_apply: Do not present per-polymer automated FF selection as literature-validated methodology; frame it as a novel design choice if implemented, and validate it empirically per family rather than by appeal to precedent.

methodology_criteria.criterion: For an aromatic-ring backbone or pendant group specifically, PCFF/CFF91's own founding validation paper documents a same-family (benzene, toluene) density deficit of -6.3%/-6.5% against experiment, with a mechanistic origin (excess NVT pressure at the true density, i.e. the nonbonded parameters are too repulsive at correct packing) rather than a sampling artifact; COMPASS reduces both compounds' error to -1.1%/-1.2% under identical conditions in the same paper. This is chemistry-matched and mechanism-verified, not a general cross-polymer reputation claim -- it is the strongest single piece of evidence in this document for a specific field switch on a specific chemistry class.
methodology_criteria.how_to_apply: When the repeat unit contains a benzene-like aromatic ring (phenyl pendant, phenylene backbone, etc.) and PCFF is the class default, treat this benzene/toluene benchmark as same-family evidence worth weighing alongside (not instead of) the class's own citations, and consider field_override='compass' as a candidate worth an admissibility check (ff_capability.py) before committing to it -- COMPASS's smaller typing-template vocabulary (96 vs PCFF's 422) means build-time admissibility must be verified per SMILES, it cannot be assumed from this benzene/toluene result. Do NOT extend this reasoning to non-aromatic chemistries -- see the PDMS counter-example above, where COMPASS is the worst of 5 fields tested and errs in the opposite direction.
methodology_criteria.evidence_strength: moderate-to-strong for aromatic chemistries specifically; not applicable outside them

methodology_criteria.criterion: For polymers whose Class-II family member (COMPASS, COMPASS II, PCFF, pcff+) has been benchmarked on the SAME polymer under a DIFFERENT Class-II variant than the class default, treat convergence or divergence between variants as informative: if two different Class-II variants land on nearly the same value for the same polymer (as with PVC bulk modulus: COMPASS 2.9470 GPa vs PolyJarvis's PCFF 2.7-2.9 GPa), that is evidence the effect is Class-II-family-wide rather than specific to the exact variant in use; if they diverge in sign (as with PEEK density: COMPASS II +2.2% over vs PolyJarvis's PCFF -5.1% under), that is evidence the effect is variant- or model-specific and should not be generalized across the Class-II family.
methodology_criteria.how_to_apply: When searching for literature support for a PCFF-routed class, do not restrict the search to 'PCFF' alone -- COMPASS, COMPASS II, and other Class-II variants on the same polymer are informative even though they are not numerically identical to PCFF; report the variant explicitly and read agreement/disagreement in this family-wide-vs-variant-specific frame rather than treating any Class-II result as interchangeable with a PCFF result.

methodology_criteria.criterion: When a literature figure surfaced by a web search summary appears to support a specific target polymer (e.g. 'PLA density error under three force fields'), trace the claim to its actual source paper and confirm what chemistry the number was actually measured on before citing it -- search-engine summarization can silently conflate a cited justification-reference (e.g. a small-molecule n-hexane benchmark used to justify a force-field choice in a PLA paper) with a finding about the target polymer itself.
methodology_criteria.how_to_apply: Before recording any reported_errors figure, verify via WebFetch that the source's OWN abstract/text states the number was measured on the polymer or analog claimed, not merely that the polymer-focused paper CITES a differently-scoped benchmark as justification; when the chemistry doesn't match (e.g. an aliphatic hydrocarbon standing in for an ester-containing polyester), exclude the claim rather than reporting it under the target polymer's name.
methodology_criteria.evidence_strength: strong (this is a documented near-miss caught during this session's own search, not a literature-derived claim)

methodology_criteria.criterion: PCFF/CFF93, OPLS-AA, and TraPPE-UA's own founding papers all validate exclusively against small molecules, model compounds, or short oligomers (up to C12 alkanes for TraPPE-UA) -- none of the three founding papers this codebase's class-routing (server.py _PCFF_CLASSES/_OPLS_CLASSES/_TRAPPE_CLASSES) ultimately rests on contains a bulk amorphous polymer-melt validation of density, Tg, or mechanical properties. This is the SAME pattern section 5 already established for COMPASS (small-molecule/PEO-only founding validation), but for PCFF/CFF93 it is narrower still on the 3 classes where it applies: the paper formally cited as ff_justification_doi on PSTR/PAMD/PSFO (in addition to the on-chemistry PCBN) is specifically a polycarbonate model-compound/crystal-structure derivation (title: 'An ab Initio CFF93 All-Atom Force Field for Polycarbonates') -- an extrapolation from ONE polymer's small-molecule fragments to three compositionally unrelated polymer chemistries, not merely from small molecules to bulk polymers in general. The remaining 11 PCFF-routed classes each cite their own separate DOI and are not affected by this specific mis-citation.
methodology_criteria.how_to_apply: Treat every current class-default force-field citation in polymer_rules.json as validating the FUNCTIONAL FORM and small-molecule parameter-fitting methodology of that force field, not as direct evidence of accuracy on any specific bulk amorphous polymer melt, unless a separate, chemistry-specific downstream paper (of the kind already collected in sections 6-15) is also cited. When routing a genuinely novel polymer to a class default, do not read the class's ff_justification_doi as polymer-melt validation by itself -- search for (or flag the absence of) chemistry-specific downstream literature exactly as sections 6-15 already do per class.

methodology_criteria.criterion: A citation whose TOPIC matches a polymer class (same chemistry family in the title/abstract) can still cite the WRONG FORCE FIELD entirely -- verify the force field actually named and used inside the paper's methods section, not just topical/chemistry match, before recording doi_verified/ff_justification_doi as meaningful support for a PCFF-routed (or any specific-FF-routed) class.
methodology_criteria.how_to_apply: When verifying or searching for a ff_justification_doi, always extract and record the specific force field name used to RUN the simulations (not merely referenced in the background/related-work section), the same way sections 7-15 and this batch (sections 20-27) already do. A chemistry-on-topic paper using a different force field family (e.g. PPHS's cited DOI, on-topic polyphosphazenes but DREIDING, not PCFF) is not evidence for the class's actual routed force field and should be flagged, not treated as validating.
methodology_criteria.evidence_strength: strong (directly demonstrated this round: PPHS's ff_justification_doi, 10.3390/polym14071451, is confirmed via full-text WebFetch to use DREIDING, not PCFF, despite being a topically on-chemistry polyphosphazene paper)

methodology_criteria.criterion: A single MD paper can report multiple, disagreeing Tg (or other property) extraction methods for the same simulated system (e.g. specific-volume-break vs self-diffusion-onset); when transcribing a literature Tg/error figure into ff_note, record which extraction method the number came from, since the paper's own preferred/most-accurate method may differ from the number already circulating in prior notes.
methodology_criteria.how_to_apply: Before transcribing a literature Tg (or density/modulus) figure, check whether the source paper computed it by more than one method and, if so, which method the authors themselves flag as more reliable; prefer that method's number, or record both with their method labels, rather than silently carrying forward whichever number was first transcribed.
methodology_criteria.evidence_strength: moderate (demonstrated this round: Wen2020/PIMN's existing ff_note cites the rho(T)-method Ultem Tg, 525K/+7.1% error, while the same paper's own D(T)-method gives 504K/+2.9% error and is explicitly called more accurate by the paper's own authors)
